## Dissertation

My research to date treats U.S. states as sites where institutions and policy choices produce unequal outcomes. In a solo-authored paper under review at *SSM - Population Health,* I use two-way fixed effects models to test whether gerrymandering is associated with infant mortality, and find that a one-standard-deviation increase in the gerrymandering measure corresponds to increases in Black, White, and total rates of infant mortality. In another working paper, I use difference-in-differences methods to study Ohio’s 2023 abortion-protection amendment; preliminary results show that it was associated with a significant reduction of anxiety and depressive symptoms among women. A third working paper examines how anti-trans laws affect the mental health of trans and gender non-conforming (TGNC) people using staggered difference-in-differences models, and finds that the first anti-trans law to pass in a state was associated with an increase in symptoms of anxiety and depression among its TGNC residents compared to TGNC residents of states which had not yet passed an anti-trans law.

## Collaborative Projects

My research program is interdisciplinary, and as such, I have sought out many interdisciplinary partnerships while at Duke. One of the main locations in which I do collaborative research currently is in the [Research in Sexual and Gender Minority Equity (RISE) Lab](https://www.theriselab.org/) under Dr. Tonia Poteat in Duke’s School of Nursing. I am co-first author on a paper under review at *Health Psychology & Behavioral Medicine* that uses structural equation modeling to assess the mediating role of stress in the relationship between experiences of discrimination and mental health problems for Black and Latina trans women living with HIV. I am also first author on a paper in progress that qualitatively examines the experiences of trans and gender non-conforming participants in a study investigating the impact of financial resources on physical and mental health; the manuscript will be the culmination of over a year’s work conducting nearly 70 in-depth interviews and analyzing responses. The other main source of collaboration for me is my participation in Dr. Hedwig Lee’s research group at Duke. As part of this lab, I am first author on a paper under review at *Population Research and Policy Review* that examines state-level race-specific trends in probation, parole, and imprisonment, and corresponding changes in infant mortality rates. In addition, I am first author on a paper soon to be submitted which investigates heterogeneity in Black birth outcomes following the police-involved killing of Amadou Diallo in the Bronx in 1999, and a main contributor to another paper which attempts to classify states into regimes of incarceration and probation and map how those regimes have changed over time using sequence analysis. My work in these research teams has allowed me to work with sociologists, epidemiologists, nurse scientists, physicians, and demographers, and that interdisciplinarity has shaped my own scholarship. It has also kept me grounded in the fact that the broad social and societal phenomena that we study as sociologists can have profound impacts on the health of populations through processes such as healthcare delivery, utilization of healthcare services, and patient decision-making.

## Future Directions

My research agenda moving forward is dedicated to understanding how states act to regulate certain bodies, and the consequences of these regulations for populations, population health, and healthcare service delivery. Over the next phase of my career, I will address the following questions:

1.  How do recent diverging trends in state laws and law enforcement, particularly laws that regulate what form bodies can take and where bodies can go (exemplified by the rise of anti-trans laws, the proliferation of abortion bans, increased pregnancy criminalization, increases in community supervision with stabilizing rates of incarceration, varying levels of cooperation with federal immigration enforcement, etc.) interact to reproduce intra- and inter-state inequalities by race, gender, and class?
2.  What are the consequences of these trends for fertility, mortality, and population health?
